--- a/minbpe/_train.py
+++ b/minbpe/_train.py
@@ -38,3 +38,25 @@
-    assert vocab_size >= 256
-    num_merges = vocab_size - 256
-    chunk_counts = {}
+    assert vocab_size >= 256
+    num_merges = vocab_size - 256
+    if vocab_size < 0x110000:
+        # all chunks (text order) in one str of code points chr(id), joined by
+        # chr(vocab_size) (never an id): pairs across it are dropped, so
+        # counts and first occurrences equal the per-chunk ones
+        sep = chr(vocab_size)
+        s = sep.join([ch.encode("utf-8").decode("latin-1")
+                      for ch in self.compiled_pattern.findall(text)])
+        stats = {}
+        _count_elements(stats, zip(s, s[1:]))
+        stats = {(ord(a), ord(b)): c for (a, b), c in stats.items()
+                 if a != sep and b != sep}
+        heap = [(-c, p) for p, c in stats.items()]
+        heapify(heap)
+        merges = {}
+        vocab = {idx: bytes([idx]) for idx in range(256)}
+        try:
+            train_str(s, num_merges, stats, heap, merges, vocab, verbose, sep)
+        except ValueError:
+            max(()) # no positive count left: max()'s own error
+        self.merges = merges
+        self.vocab = vocab
+        return
+    chunk_counts = {}

actions.reason: I tried running RegexTokenizer.train's merges through the C str.replace path that BasicTokenizer training already uses, with all chunks joined by a separator. Outputs were identical, but train_ir went up (ratio 1.114) because joining the chunks gives up the chunk dedup. That result also shows the Python per-chunk merge loop is only a small share of train_ir, which is mostly fixed interpreter, regex and harness cost. Earlier attempts on encode_ir (presence checks) and on train's initial counting (C helpers) also made things slower. I've reverted the change and found no 1% win I could measure.

journal.text:
I tried moving RegexTokenizer.train's merge step onto the C str.replace path that BasicTokenizer training already uses. I joined all chunks with a separator so each merge became one replace call, then edited minbpe/_train.py to wire it in and trimmed it back down.

Both builds were ok and outputs were identical, but my sandbox run rejected it. train_ir went from 310367198 to 345745256, ratio 1.1140 against a required 0.9900. encode_ir stayed at ratio 1.0000. Joining the chunks throws away the chunk dedup, and that cost more than the faster replace saved. I gave up and submitted nothing.

I now believe the Python per-chunk merge loop is only a small share of train_ir. Most of it looks like fixed interpreter and setup cost, so speeding up the merge loop alone will not reach the threshold.

Next I want to profile train_ir by phase before editing anything. If merges matter at all, I would keep the dedup by replacing over unique chunks weighted by their counts rather than over the joined corpus.
